slots.practicalActivity: Pick 5 real files or tables you have access to (or tables from AdventureWorks2012, used in this course's SQL labs). For each, list its metadata without opening or querying it, then classify each metadata fact as business, technical, or operational metadata. Finally, note which naming or documentation standard -- an existing one, or one you'd propose -- would govern how that metadata gets captured going forward.
slots.deliverable: A table of 5 items, each with 3+ metadata facts correctly labeled business/technical/operational, plus a one-sentence proposed or existing standard for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Walk one real table you have access to through the metadata management lifecycle stages (capture, maintain, govern, retire), writing one sentence for each stage describing what actually happens to its metadata today. Then research one real metadata repository or catalog tool (Microsoft Purview, Collibra, or even a plain SQL Server extended-properties approach) and describe, stage by stage, where that table's metadata would actually get stored in it.
slots.deliverable: A 4-stage lifecycle walkthrough for one real table, each stage mapped to where it would live in a named repository tool.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice: using AdventureWorks2012 (or another SQL Server instance from this course's SQL labs), run sp_help or query INFORMATION_SCHEMA against 3 real tables you haven't examined yet, and for each one produce one business-metadata fact, one technical-metadata fact, and one operational-metadata fact.
slots.deliverable: A worksheet covering 3 real tables, each with one correctly-labeled business, technical, and operational metadata fact.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick 3 real business terms from your own work or AdventureWorks2012 (for example, Active Customer, Net Revenue, On-Time Order). Write a first-draft definition for each, then run every draft through the four-part test from this chapter (specific, self-contained, measurable where possible, free of implementation detail) and rewrite any definition that fails one of the four.
slots.deliverable: 3 term definitions shown in before/after form, with the specific test each failing draft didn't pass, and the corrected version.

slots.practicalActivity: For the 3 terms you refined in the previous slot, assign a named steward role (a role, like "VP Sales" or "Finance Data Owner" -- not a specific person) accountable for approving each one, and sketch a one-step approval workflow. Then link at least 2 of the terms together with a related-term or hierarchy relationship.
slots.deliverable: A glossary governance sheet: 3 terms, each with an assigned steward role and approval step, plus at least one related-term link between two of them.

slots.practicalActivity: Build an actual mini business glossary: take the 3 terms you've refined so far plus 2 new ones from the same business domain, and lay all 5 out in a spreadsheet or document with columns for Term, Definition, Steward, Status (draft/approved), and Related Terms -- the structure a real tool like Microsoft Purview or Collibra would use.
slots.deliverable: A 5-term business glossary spreadsheet or document with every required column filled in for each term.

slots.practicalActivity: Query INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS (or sys.columns) against 2 real tables in AdventureWorks2012, pulling the structural facts -- data type, nullability, max length -- for every column. Then draft a one-page data dictionary standard (required fields, naming rules, format for descriptions) that your documentation will follow going forward.
slots.deliverable: INFORMATION_SCHEMA query output documenting every column of 2 real tables, plus a one-page written data dictionary standard.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the standard from the previous slot, build a complete data dictionary entry for every column of one AdventureWorks2012 table (for example, Sales.SalesOrderHeader), attaching a glossary-linked description for at least 2 columns via sp_addextendedproperty or a spreadsheet column. Then write a one-paragraph process describing who updates each entry when that table's schema changes.
slots.deliverable: A complete data dictionary covering every column of one real table, with at least 2 glossary-term links, plus a written maintenance process.

slots.practicalActivity: Hands-on lab: pick a second, unfamiliar table in AdventureWorks2012 or AdventureWorksDW2014 that you haven't documented yet, and build its full data dictionary from scratch end to end -- query its real schema, write standard-compliant entries for every column, and link at least 2 columns to glossary terms from the previous chapter -- without referring back to the lesson videos.
slots.deliverable: A complete, standard-compliant data dictionary for one new real table, with at least 2 glossary-term links.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick 4 real columns from AdventureWorks2012 tables you've documented in earlier slots. Walk each one through the four Critical Data Element criteria -- regulatory relevance, financial materiality, decision impact, downstream reach -- deciding which columns qualify as CDEs, then rank the qualifying ones in priority order.
slots.deliverable: A worksheet scoring 4 real columns against the four CDE criteria, with a ranked priority list of whichever columns qualify.

lessons.title: Critical Data Elements and Regulatory Reporting

slots.practicalActivity: For the top-ranked CDE from the previous slot, produce its elevated documentation package: a named source system of record, a validation rule, and an escalation contact. Then write one paragraph explaining which regulatory, financial, or executive report that column would realistically feed, and why its CDE status is justified.
slots.deliverable: A completed CDE documentation package for one real column, plus a paragraph connecting it to a specific regulatory or executive report.

slots.practicalActivity: Research one real data catalog tool (Microsoft Purview, Collibra, or Alation) and compare its search and browse capabilities against what a catalog is supposed to deliver for findability. Then sketch how 2 of the glossary and dictionary entries you've already built in this course would appear as catalog entries inside that tool.
slots.deliverable: A short written comparison of one real catalog tool's search capabilities, plus a sketch of how 2 of your own entries would look cataloged in it.

slots.practicalActivity: Combine the data dictionary and glossary entries you've built across this course into 2 unified catalog entries (business metadata plus technical metadata together) for 2 real tables. Then run a metadata quality check against each entry -- completeness, accuracy, freshness -- and flag any gaps you find.
slots.deliverable: 2 combined catalog entries plus a completed metadata-quality checklist for each, with any gaps flagged.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the Hartwell Logistics case study's adoption tactic -- embedding the catalog link inside an existing dashboard people already use, rather than hoping they discover a new destination -- write a one-paragraph adoption plan for getting your own 2 catalog entries from the previous slot actually used by the people who'd need them.
slots.deliverable: A one-paragraph catalog adoption plan grounded in the case study's "embed it where people already look" tactic, applied to your own catalog entries.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page, chapter-by-chapter walkthrough -- in the style of the Hartwell Logistics case study -- applying every chapter of this course (metadata types, business glossary, data dictionary, Critical Data Elements, data catalog) to one real recurring "which number is right" disagreement from your own work, a class project, or AdventureWorks2012 data.
slots.deliverable: A one-page written case-study walkthrough covering all 5 chapters applied to one real or realistic disagreement.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can write glossary-quality business term definitions, build a real data dictionary directly from a database's own schema, identify and document Critical Data Elements, and assemble those pieces into catalog entries that other people can actually find and trust.
